segments.say: Ivy turns onto her side and pulls the blanket a little higher, as if someone could see her blushing in the dark. Nobody can, of course. The room is empty except for her and a stack of library books on the chair. But her body is behaving as though the lecture hall were right here, with all those faces turned her way. A memory has reached out of the past and into her cheeks.

This is one of the most curious things about embarrassment. You can't really have it only in your head. It spills over into the face, the eyes, the shoulders and the hands. People squeeze their eyes shut, or cover their mouths, or let out a groan, or even say no out loud to an empty room. Researchers have studied these reactions closely, and they turn out to follow a surprisingly regular pattern.

In 1995, the psychologist Dacher Keltner published a study in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology called Signs of Appeasement. He carefully coded the faces and movements of people in embarrassing moments, frame by frame. He found that embarrassment has its own recognisable display, distinct from amusement and distinct from shame. It isn't just a messy jumble of reactions. It unfolds in a typical order.

show.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 1995

segments.say: Here's roughly what Keltner described. First, the eyes look down. Then a smile appears, but it's a smile that tries to hide itself, with the lips pressed or pulled to the side. The head turns down and away. And quite often, a hand comes up to touch the face. You've almost certainly done every one of these, maybe in a single second, without ever deciding to.

show.title: The embarrassment display
items: A smile that tries to hide itself
The head turns down and away
A hand often touches the face

segments.say: Picture someone who has just walked into a glass door, or called their teacher by the wrong name. You can almost see it. The glance at the floor, the crooked smile, the hand rising to the forehead. It's a face we all know, from every culture we meet. And that's a clue. A display that regular is usually doing a job.

In 1997, Keltner and his colleague Brenda Buswell published a review in Psychological Bulletin that pulled the research together. Their idea was that embarrassment has an appeasement function. In plain words, it works like a small, wordless apology. It tells the people around us that we know we slipped, that we care about the rules, and that we're not a threat to the group.

So when Ivy, at 19, dropped her hand and looked down at her notebook with a little embarrassed smile, she wasn't failing. She was saying something to everyone nearby, without a single word. Oops, my mistake, I know. And that's a message other people are very good at reading, and usually very quick to forgive.

Long before brain scans, Charles Darwin was fascinated by one part of this display in particular. In his book The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals, published in 1872, he wrote that blushing is the most peculiar and the most human of all expressions. He noticed that we can't blush on purpose, and that simply being looked at, or thinking we are being looked at, can bring it on.

show.text: Blushing is the most peculiar and the most human of all expressions.

segments.say: That point of Darwin's matters more than it might seem. Most expressions can be faked, at least a little. You can put on a polite smile. But very few people can blush on command. And a signal that's hard to fake is a signal other people tend to believe. When someone blushes, we know, almost instinctively, that they really do feel it.

show.sub: A signal that's hard to forge

segments.say: Ivy can feel that warmth now, spreading across her face in the dark, like a lamp someone else has switched on. It's a strange thing, to blush alone, for an audience that isn't there. But it shows how powerfully the brain can replay the social side of a memory. It doesn't just remember what happened. It remembers what it felt like to be seen.

show.cap: A warm glow you can't switch off

segments.say: Here's one way to think about it. The blush is the body remembering that other people matter. Even alone in the dark, years later, Ivy's cheeks still warm because some deep part of her still cares how she seemed to a room full of near strangers. That isn't foolish. It's a sign of a mind that was built for living alongside others, and takes that job seriously.

show.text: The blush is the body remembering that other people matter.

segments.say: And here's something even stranger. You don't even need to be the one who slipped. Have you ever watched someone on television make a painful mistake, and found yourself wincing, or looking away, or reaching for the remote? Many of us feel embarrassed for other people. Psychologists call it vicarious embarrassment, and some of them have looked at it inside the brain.

In 2011, a team led by Sören Krach in Germany published a study in the journal PLoS ONE with a memorable title. Your flaws are my pain. They showed volunteers in a brain scanner pictures and short descriptions of people in awkward, embarrassing situations. When the volunteers felt embarrassed on someone else's behalf, two regions were especially active, the anterior cingulate cortex and the anterior insula.

show.what: Watching others slip activates pain-linked regions

segments.say: Those two regions come up again and again in research on empathy, including our response to other people's pain. That doesn't mean watching an awkward moment is the same as being hurt. But it does suggest that the brain handles other people's social stumbles in some of the same places where it handles feeling for them. The cringe, in other words, is partly a form of caring.

Put together, vicarious embarrassment tells us something quite lovely about people. We feel social moments in our bodies. We easily take other people's point of view. We care how others are treated by the group. And we know the unwritten rules well enough to feel it when they're broken. The same sensitive machinery is running when Ivy cringes at her own old memory.

show.title: What vicarious embarrassment tells us
items: We feel social moments in the body
We care how others are treated

segments.say: Notice how differently we judge those other people, though. When you see someone on a show wave at a person who wasn't waving at them, do you think they're a fool? Usually not. You think, oh no, poor thing, I've done that too. We give strangers a warmth and a quick forgiveness that we rarely give to our own younger selves.

Ivy tries something, almost without meaning to. She pictures the lecture hall again, but this time she pictures it as if she were sitting a few rows back, watching some other girl wave. And from back there, the moment looks completely different. It's sweet. It's a little funny. It's the kind of thing you'd smile at, and then forget about entirely by lunchtime.

Here's a thought to hold onto. We are often the only ones still keeping score. Everyone who saw that wave had their own lecture to follow, their own worries, their own coat and lunch and plans. They may have smiled for a second. Then their minds moved on. Only one person in that room has carried the moment for nearly ten years, and she was the one who made it.

show.text: We are often the only ones still keeping score.

segments.say: If we could ask the students who saw Ivy's wave, what would they say they felt? Most likely a flicker of recognition. A small, kind smile. Perhaps a passing memory of the time they did something just like it. And then, almost straight away, their attention went back to the lecture, the notes and the morning. That's the whole of it.

show.title: What the watchers probably felt
items: A memory of their own slip

segments.say: There's something tender in looking back at a younger self this way. At 19, Ivy was new to the city, a little nervous, eager to be friendly, and still learning the quiet rules of a big lecture hall. If a 19-year-old friend told Ivy this story today, she wouldn't think less of her at all. She'd probably laugh softly, and say, oh, I love that, I've done exactly that.

show.sub: The girl she used to be

segments.say: And her younger self handled it perfectly well, really. The eyes went down, the smile went sideways, the cheeks went pink. The wordless apology was sent and received. The lecture began. Life continued. The display did exactly what it was designed to do. It's only the memory, replaying in the dark, that never quite got the message that it's over.

Which brings us to a question that feels almost too simple to ask. How closely were those people watching, anyway? When we replay an embarrassing moment, we usually picture every face turned toward us, every eye noticing every detail. But is that what really happens? Or is the audience in our memory much bigger, and much sharper-eyed, than the audience that was actually there?

That question has been tested in some wonderfully simple experiments. And their answer is one of the most comforting things in all of social psychology. So let's leave the warm glow of the blush behind for a moment, and turn toward the audience itself.
